title: Diabetic ketoacidosis (child)
subject: paediatrics
summary: Glucose above 200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L), venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L, and ketonaemia: 0.9% saline 10 to 20 mL/kg over 20 to 30 minutes, replace the deficit over 24 to 48 hours, start IV insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h 1 hour after fluids with potassium, and watch hourly for cerebral oedema (ISPAD 2022).

sections.title: Diagnose and grade
items: Diagnosis: blood glucose above 200 mg/dL (11 mmol/L), venous pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L, and ketonaemia (beta-hydroxybutyrate 3 mmol/L or more) or moderate to large ketonuria.
Severity: mild pH below 7.3 or bicarbonate below 18 mmol/L; moderate pH below 7.2 or bicarbonate below 10; severe pH below 7.1 or bicarbonate below 5 mmol/L.

Clinical: dehydration, deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing, vomiting, abdominal pain that can mimic an acute abdomen, drowsiness. Weak or impalpable pulses, hypotension or oliguria suggest dehydration of 10% or more.

HHS: glucose above 600 mg/dL (33.3 mmol/L), venous pH above 7.25, bicarbonate above 15 mmol/L, effective osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, little ketosis. It needs larger fluid volumes (bolus 20 mL/kg or more) and delayed, lower-dose insulin; manage in ICU.

sections.title: First hour
items: ABC; oxygen if circulation is impaired; two peripheral IV lines (avoid central lines); cardiac monitor; weigh the child. Protect the airway if consciousness is severely reduced.

Volume depleted but not in shock: 0.9% saline 10 to 20 mL/kg over 20 to 30 minutes (20 mL/kg if perfusion is poor). Shock (rare): 0.9% saline 20 mL/kg boluses as fast as possible, reassessing after each.

Send glucose, blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, venous gas, sodium, potassium, chloride, urea, creatinine, calcium, phosphate, magnesium and CBC; ECG if potassium will be delayed. Look for and treat infection.
Do not give an IV insulin bolus. Start the insulin infusion at least 1 hour after IV fluids have begun.

Manage in PICU or an equivalent unit if DKA is severe, circulation is compromised, consciousness is depressed, or cerebral oedema risk is high (age under 5 years, pH below 7.1, pCO2 below 21 mmHg, urea nitrogen above 20 mg/dL).

sections.title: Fluids and electrolytes
items: After the bolus, replace the estimated deficit (assume 5 to 10% dehydration) minus the bolus volume over 24 to 48 hours, plus maintenance, using 0.45% to 0.9% saline or a balanced solution (Ringer lactate, Plasma-Lyte). Do not routinely add urine losses.
Obese children: calculate as for other children; if volumes exceed adult protocols, use adult limits (1 L maximum per bolus, 500 mL/h).

Potassium: add 40 mmol/L to the infusate when starting insulin. If potassium is above 5.5 mmol/L, wait for urine output and add it once below 5.5. If potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L at presentation, start replacement with the first fluids, defer insulin, and give potassium no faster than 0.5 mmol/kg/h with cardiac monitoring.

Use a mix of potassium chloride with potassium phosphate or acetate (for example 20 mmol/L each) to limit hyperchloraemic acidosis. Treat severe hypophosphataemia (below 1 mg/dL, 0.32 mmol/L) with potassium phosphate while monitoring calcium.
Do not give bicarbonate except for life-threatening hyperkalaemia or venous pH below 6.9 with impaired cardiac contractility.

sections.title: Insulin and glucose
items: Regular (soluble) insulin IV 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h; 0.05 units/kg/h is enough if pH is above 7.15, and 0.03 units/kg/h may suffice in mild DKA under 5 years. Example: 50 units in 50 mL 0.9% saline (1 unit/mL); flush the tubing with the solution first.

Keep insulin at this rate until DKA resolves (pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 18 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate below 1 mmol/L or anion gap closed). Ketones should fall by about 0.5 mmol/L per hour; if not, reassess and increase insulin.

Add 5% dextrose when glucose falls to about 250 to 300 mg/dL (14 to 17 mmol/L), or sooner if it falls by more than 90 mg/dL (5 mmol/L) per hour. Use 10% or 12.5% dextrose if needed rather than cutting insulin while acidosis persists.

If IV infusion is not possible, in mild to moderate DKA with good perfusion: subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.15 units/kg every 2 hours, starting 1 hour after fluids (reduce to 0.1 units/kg if glucose falls over 90 mg/dL per hour despite dextrose).

Transition when ketoacidosis has resolved and oral intake is tolerated: give subcutaneous insulin including a basal dose, ideally before a meal, with rapid-acting insulin 15 to 30 minutes before stopping the infusion.

sections.title: Monitoring
items: Hourly: heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, GCS and neurological observations, insulin dose, all fluid input and output, and capillary glucose (cross-check with laboratory glucose).

Every 2 to 4 hours: electrolytes, glucose, urea, calcium, magnesium, phosphate and blood gas; blood ketones every 2 hours where available. Urine ketones lag and should not be used to judge resolution.

Anion gap = sodium minus (chloride + bicarbonate): normal about 12 mmol/L, typically 20 to 30 in DKA. A low bicarbonate with falling ketones is usually benign hyperchloraemic acidosis and should not delay transition.

sections.title: Cerebral oedema (cerebral injury)
items: Keep mannitol or 3% saline, with the dose calculated, at the bedside for children at high risk: age under 5 years, new-onset diabetes, pH below 7.1, pCO2 below 21 mmHg, or urea nitrogen above 20 mg/dL. Most cases occur in the first 12 hours of treatment.

Warning signs after treatment starts: new or worsening headache, vomiting, heart rate slowing not explained by volume or sleep, irritability, confusion, incontinence, cranial nerve palsy, falling SpO2. Hypertension alone is not a warning sign.

Bedside diagnosis: one diagnostic criterion (abnormal motor or verbal response to pain, decorticate or decerebrate posture, cranial nerve III, IV or VI palsy, abnormal neurogenic breathing), or two major, or one major and two minor criteria.

Treat immediately: mannitol 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes (repeat after 30 minutes if needed) or 3% saline 2.5 to 5 mL/kg over 10 to 15 minutes; elevate the head, keep blood pressure normal without excess fluid, and call PICU. Do imaging only after treatment has started.

sections.title: Prevent recurrence
items: DKA in a child with known diabetes is almost always due to missed insulin or interrupted pump delivery: review sick-day rules, ketone testing, insulin supply, storage and psychosocial issues before discharge.
New diagnosis: educate the family and ensure reliable access to insulin, glucose and ketone testing, and diabetes team follow-up.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Giving an insulin bolus or starting insulin before fluids.
Stopping or reducing insulin because glucose has normalised, instead of adding dextrose.
Treating hyperchloraemic acidosis as ongoing ketoacidosis.
Restricting fluids so much that circulation is compromised; the PECARN FLUID trial found faster versus slower rehydration did not change cerebral injury rates.

drugs.name: 0.9% sodium chloride (bolus)
drugs.dose: 10 to 20 mL/kg IV over 20 to 30 minutes; 20 mL/kg boluses as fast as possible if in shock
drugs.notes: Then deficit replacement over 24 to 48 hours with 0.45% to 0.9% saline or balanced solution plus maintenance.

drugs.name: Regular (soluble) insulin infusion
drugs.dose: 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h IV, started at least 1 hour after fluids
drugs.notes: No bolus. Continue until pH above 7.30, bicarbonate above 18 mmol/L and ketones below 1 mmol/L.

drugs.name: Rapid-acting insulin analogue (subcutaneous)
drugs.notes: Only for mild to moderate DKA with good perfusion when IV infusion is not possible.

drugs.name: Potassium chloride / phosphate
drugs.dose: 40 mmol/L in IV fluid; maximum rate 0.5 mmol/kg/h
drugs.notes: Start with insulin once potassium is below 5.5 mmol/L and urine is passed; earlier if hypokalaemic.

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
drugs.dose: 0.5 to 1 g/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes; may repeat after 30 minutes

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 3%
drugs.dose: 2.5 to 5 mL/kg IV over 10 to 15 minutes
drugs.notes: Alternative to mannitol, or if no response to mannitol in 15 to 30 minutes.
